title: Database Concurrency Control: Serializability, Locking, MVCC and OCC
summary: Quick revision notes on how databases keep concurrent transactions correct: serializability and conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking, deadlocks, MVCC snapshots and optimistic concurrency, ending with a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Serializability Mental Model
points: Serializable schedule: an interleaved execution whose result equals some serial (one-at-a-time) order of the same transactions
Two operations conflict only if they touch the same item, come from different transactions, and at least one is a write (R-W, W-R, W-W; R-R never conflicts)
Conflict serializable: a schedule that can be turned into a serial one by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations

Precedence graph test: one node per transaction, edge Ti→Tj if an op of Ti conflicts with and precedes an op of Tj; acyclic means conflict serializable, and a topological order gives the equivalent serial order
Conflict serializable is a subset of serializable (view serializable also admits blind writes); engines enforce only the conflict form because it is cheap to test

chapters.title: Shared and Exclusive Locks
points: Shared (S) lock for reading: many transactions can hold S on the same item at once
Exclusive (X) lock for writing: only one holder, and it blocks every other S and X request
Compatibility matrix: S+S is allowed; S+X, X+S and X+X are blocked, so the requester waits
Lock upgrade S→X on the same item succeeds only if no other transaction holds S; two transactions upgrading the same item deadlock
Locks alone do not give serializability: releasing a lock right after each operation still allows non-serializable interleavings (lost update, unrepeatable read)

chapters.title: Two-Phase Locking and Deadlocks
points: 2PL rule: a transaction has a growing phase (only acquires locks) then a shrinking phase (only releases); after the first unlock it can never lock again
Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, with the lock point (the moment the last lock is acquired) giving the serial order
Strict 2PL holds all X locks until commit/abort, preventing dirty reads and cascading aborts; strong strict (rigorous) 2PL holds S locks as well; real engines use these
2PL does not prevent deadlock: T1 holds A and waits for B while T2 holds B and waits for A
Detection: build a wait-for graph and abort a victim (usually the cheapest or youngest) when a cycle appears; a lock timeout is the crude alternative
Prevention: acquire locks in one global order, or use wait-die / wound-wait with timestamps; after a deadlock abort, the application must retry the transaction

chapters.title: MVCC Snapshots
points: MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row; every write creates a new version stamped with its transaction ID and keeps the old version (in the heap in PostgreSQL, in the undo log in InnoDB and Oracle, which update the row in place)
A reader sees a consistent snapshot as of its start (or statement start) and takes no read locks, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers
Writers still conflict with each other: two writes to the same row serialize via a row lock, and the second waits or fails
Snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, Oracle) allows write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, update different rows, and break an invariant (both doctors go off call)
Old versions must be cleaned up (PostgreSQL VACUUM, InnoDB purge); a long-running transaction pins old versions and bloats storage
Fix write skew with true serializable (PostgreSQL SSI aborts one transaction), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a constraint

chapters.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
points: OCC takes no locks while running: read, compute on private copies, then validate at commit and abort on conflict
Three phases: read (work on local copy), validate (check no other transaction changed what you read or wrote), write (apply changes)
Application pattern: add a version column and run UPDATE t SET ..., version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?; zero rows affected means a conflict, so re-read and retry
Pessimistic locking (2PL, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) wins under high contention; OCC wins under low contention and long think-time (web forms), since aborted work is wasted
Always check the affected-row count and bound the retries with backoff; ignoring the count silently loses updates

chapters.title: Concurrency Control Cheat Sheet
points: Conflict = same item + different transactions + at least one write; precedence graph acyclic ⇒ conflict serializable
Lock compat: S+S ok, everything involving X blocks; upgrade S→X can deadlock
2PL = grow then shrink; Strict 2PL = hold X locks until commit; deadlock fix = global lock order, wait-for-graph victim, or retry
MVCC: readers do not block writers; snapshot isolation still allows write skew, so use SERIALIZABLE or FOR UPDATE
Pick pessimistic locks for hot rows and OCC with a version column for rare conflicts; always retry aborted transactions
